questions.question: Explain the following periodic irregularities: (a) the first ionisation enthalpy of Mg is greater than that of Al although Mg is to the left of Al. (b) The atomic radius of Na is greater than that of Cl.
questions.solution:
**(a) $I_1(\text{Mg}) > I_1(\text{Al})$**

$$\text{Mg}: [\text{Ne}]\,3s^2 \qquad \text{Al}: [\text{Ne}]\,3s^24p^1$$

The first electron removed from Mg comes from a completely filled $3s$ subshell, which is a particularly stable arrangement. In Al the first electron is the $3p$ electron, which is higher in energy, is shielded by the $3s$ pair and is repelled less. Since Mg's valence electron is more tightly held, $I_1(\text{Mg}) = 596$ kJ mol⁻¹ and $I_1(\text{Al}) = 578$ kJ mol⁻¹.

**(b) $r(\text{Na}) > r(\text{Cl})$**

Na and Cl are in the same period, so the number of shells is the same (n = 3). Across a period the nuclear charge increases from Na (Z = 11) to Cl (Z = 17) while the added electrons go into the same shell, so effective nuclear charge per electron rises. The stronger pull draws the cloud closer, so the radius falls.

$$r(\text{Na}) = 186 \ \text{pm} > r(\text{Cl}) = 99 \ \text{pm}$$
questions.knowledgeNote: A filled s subshell is extra stable, so Mg resists ionisation more than the higher 3p electron of aluminium.
